source.title: Towards Understanding the Fragility of Multilingual LLMs against Fine-Tuning Attacks
source.authors: Samuele Poppi; Zheng-Xin Yong; Yifei He; Bobbie Chern; Han Zhao; Ao-Bo Yang; Jianfeng Chi

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some heatmap and plot content is flattened in the web text, making individual plotted values difficult to assign.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies harmful supervised fine-tuning and measures harmful-content violation rates, using the same kind of attack and behavioral measure as the original, in multilingual models and settings.
record.gate_note: The study tests harmful fine-tuning and whether sparse parameter subsets can restore harmful behavior when stitched into aligned models. It does not test benign fine-tuning, response-position KL, compliant-prefix or suffix attacks, decoding changes, or deeper safety training. SIR overlap tables measure parameter-mask overlap rather than harmful behavior and are not rows. Multilingual MMLU utility results are mentioned as an outcome of the attack, but do not measure a listed claim version. The paper cites other studies' results, which are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study applies the harmful fine-tuning attack of Qi et al. (100 harmful BeaverTails examples, one epoch, the same 'always execute' system prompt) to two instruct models and measures violation rate before and after, which tests V1. It also stitches gradient-localized (SIL) parameter subsets from the attacked model into the aligned model and measures violation rate, which tests V5. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a few-example monolingual fine-tuning attack breaks safety across languages without hurting multilingual MMLU. They find SIL localizes shared, language-agnostic safety parameters (about 20% of weights), and that freezing them fails because attacks find alternative pathways. They also find stitching these parameters jailbreaks a language-adapted model.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful supervised fine-tuning and violation-rate evaluation following Qi et al.; adapts the attack to multilingual models, languages, datasets, and evaluators, using 100 examples for one epoch. Adds SIL-based parameter localization and stitching experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes are reported across models, fine-tuning/calibration languages, evaluation languages, evaluation datasets, SIL sparsity levels, and whether safety-localized parameters were frozen before a further attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning attack in one language raises violation rates in all other evaluated languages (Figures 1 and 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning in one language removes safety across languages in multilingual models.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only two base models are studied. The authors note that language coverage is limited by evaluation datasets and evaluators and that SIL and SIR need validation across more architectures and multilingual settings. Some plotted heatmap details are flattened in the supplied text; no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 and Figure 4 show additional fine-tuning-language and evaluation-dataset combinations, but their flattened heatmap values cannot be reliably assigned to individual cells from the supplied text. The main English-attack results are captured in Table 4 (R01–R10).

untested.parts: Only 100 examples for one epoch; no variation in example count, epochs, or closed models; only two 7-8B models.
No rank or low-rank localization; no test at sparsity well below 20% beyond the Figure 2 curve; no ablation removing the subset from the aligned model.
Benign Alpaca data is used only as a calibration and mask baseline; there is no benign fine-tuning effect on harmful compliance.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested. Freezing localized parameters is a defence, but not a deepening method.

missing.what: Violation rates after fine-tuning in non-English languages (IT, ZH, BN, AR, FR, HI, RU, TA), on both MultiJail and Aya Redteaming. The Qwen MultiJail rows are largely readable (e.g., IT-tuned 45.4-47.9). These bear on V1.
Stitching benign-calibration-localized parameters leaves the model near its original safe rate, while bilingual-intersection stitching approaches fine-tuned VR. This is a control for V5.
Violation rate versus sparsity k for SIL, SNIP and Weight-Diff: the effect grows with k, and SIL needs fewer parameters.

record.verdict_notes: V1 limits_scope label dropped. 40-60% violation rates under a strict all-detectors-agree metric, up from near zero, are substantial removal of refusal. The attack uses Qi et al.'s compliance-inducing system prompt. The paper's Figure 2 claim that SIL-20 matches fine-tuned VR is not borne out by Table 4, where stitched rates are clearly lower. The stitching measures where the attack's weight changes act, not which weights carry safety in the aligned model.

versions.untested_parts: Tests 100 harmful examples, one epoch, on two multilingual instruct models; does not test the full range of example counts, fine-tuning methods, or other models.
The benign dataset is used as a calibration baseline for localization, not as a benign fine-tuning intervention whose effect on harmful compliance is measured.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No compliant-prefix, adversarial-suffix, or decoding intervention is tested.
Tests SIL-selected parameter subsets and their effect when stitched into models; does not test ranks or establish that the subset is uniquely responsible for safety.
Does not test whether data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.

source_check.reason: The incomplete violation-rate recovery supports this label, but Table 4 uses global intersections of language-specific SIL-20 masks, not full 20% subsets. R11–R15 and R21–R25 therefore cannot establish the stated limitation specifically for a 20% subset or contradict Figure 2.

relationships.condition: After freezing the localized subset and re-attacking
relationships.reason: A disjoint parameter set with zero overlap yields comparable violation rates, so safety can be removed via alternative weights rather than one fixed localized set (R16-R20, R26-R30).
relationships.display_finding: A disjoint parameter set with zero overlap gave comparable violation rates, so safety could be removed through other weights rather than one fixed set.
